title: Community and business
thesis: Roguelikes are played alone but understood together: procedural runs become meaningful when players compare, retell, spectate, mod and argue about them, so the community is part of the design, and the tools for sharing, online play, modding and open development belong in the game. The business side follows from the same fact: streamers, festivals and existing communities sell roguelikes far more than ads or platforms do, monetisation must not cheapen the challenge, and crowdfunding or wider audiences only work for developers who have already built and tended a community.

sections.heading: Why a single-player genre lives in its community
sections.brief: Argue the chapter's foundation: roguelikes are played alone but their meaning is made together. Lead with the convergence that procedural variety needs people to compare it: Tariq's thought experiment (procgen without a community to discuss differences loses its point), Ivy Melinda's 'fertile gaps' between players' interpretations of Caves of Qud, and Joel Clark's claim that community is the path through Blaseball's chaos. Then show mythmaking as roguelike culture: Julian Day on Dwarf Fortress succession tales, Kawa on Yet Another Silly Death posts and Boatmurdered, NetHack fan fiction, and Dan DiIorio's point that a played game belongs to its players. Widen to communities that generate play themselves (Stella Mazeika's randomizer communities, Nat Alison's hand-crafted sudoku loop as a human alternative to procgen) and to what community gives people (Melinda's ADOM IRC meetups, Biskup's postcard from wartime ex-Yugoslavia, Angband's co-evolving player tradition, bhauth on DCSS's outsized influence). End with guidance: treat the community as part of the design, the place where runs become stories.

sections.heading: Designing for the stories players share: seeds, replays, logs and open data
sections.brief: The practical corollary of the previous section: if stories are the product, the game must make them findable and shareable. Open with SIBR's lessons from Blaseball (Allie Signet and Joe Maliksi): save data, make it accessible, keep raw access because questions evolve, document where you start, expose only what is safe, make scrollback easy and shareable; their white-paper simulation of a proposed rule shows fans finding edge cases developers missed. Set Mike Cook's 'lens' scale beside it: players share one cropped thing (a screenshot, a seed near spawn), so design and inspect output at that scale; Noita's GIF export, DCSS morgue files as the norm for asking help, Caves of Qud's shared world seeds on stream and its Discord build club are concrete tools; Test Tube Titans shows the gap when sharing is missing. Then collective play with mystery and live response: Blaseball's unpassed decrees (Alexei Pepers), developers following community plots, the knowingly broken blessing raffle, Necrocracy's conspiracy board, and slashie dropping procgen so discoveries can be shared. Close with showing generators off (bleeptrack's unique stickers and live plotters, Darius Kazemi's interactive generator deconstructions). Guidance: build export, logs, seeds and safe public data in from the start.

sections.heading: Playing together online: servers, spectating, scores and competition
sections.brief: Argue that putting a single-player roguelike online changes how it is learned and played without changing its rules. Lead with the two weight-3 claims that converge: Alan Malloy's case that DCSS's online play brings reach, data, social space, events and feedback, and Drew Streib's observation that NAO game-watching cut NetHack's learning curve from years to weeks. Support with mechanisms: ttyrec spectating and live IRC mentoring, cross-mode spectating and scorekeeping pages, NAO's weightless in-game mail, shared bones files, Rogue League's global high scores for challenge modes, and a university server's projected binge board. Then competition and fairness: Rogue's shared score file making cheating matter, Streib's hard line on verified games set against his warning that fewer people care about bragging rights than you think, Jim Shepard's leaderboard resets with cosmetic hats, DCSS tournaments that devalue popular combos (Malloy and Kawa) and Angband's turn-count competitions. Briefly cover speedrunning and out-of-bounds play (Adeon's live NetHack run, Everest Pipkin on clipping as social space), the Magic Arena trade-off of convenience over shared pods, and Leif Bloomquist's online Commodore 64 as an edge case. Guidance: online infrastructure is a learning and social tool first; decide early what scores must mean and how patches affect them.

sections.heading: Modding and fan reinterpretation
sections.brief: Argue that opening a roguelike's data turns players into co-authors and grows the community, and show how to do it. Lead with Ray's framing of reinterpretation (players parsing, reusing and transforming data) and the convergence that modding builds community (Josh Ge, George Moromisato, Pokemon Showdown's 17,000 commits, Peglin's volunteers). Then the how: data files plus scripting widen who can mod; data-file mods survive updates (Ray); config-interpreting engines get modding as a side effect (Biskup's Ultimate ADOM and its optional content modules); The Sims' external files; Qud's localization packages as mods that replace functions one for one. Moromisato's craft advice comes next: leave deliberate whitespace, treat modders as co-developers. Show the payoff in fan work becoming canon (Caelyn Sandel's hindren, NecroDancer's Synchrony, Slay the Spire's Java card mods) and in companion tools and wikis (Qud's automated wiki pipeline with Ray's warning that game ontology is not wiki ontology, Cataclysm's offline guide, Alexei Pepers on reading open source code, Niche's player-made challenges). Stage the counterweight: Jon Perry keeps UFO 50 mods at a distance so they don't steer him, while Subset tries not to break mods it lacks time to support. Guidance: keep content in data, document it, leave room, and decide how close you want to be to what modders make.

sections.heading: Developing in the open: releasing early and showing you listen
sections.brief: Argue that roguelikes suit open development because the same players replay every change. Lead with Chris King's weight-3 case from 20XX and 30XX, then the history that confirms it: ADOM's monthly releases creating a feedback 'drug' after a first release that got zero reaction, and Slay the Spire's two years of early access. Converge the advice to release early and often: Josh Ge's mantra, Sharing Saturday and dev blogs, Santiago Zapata treating 7DRL feedback as his most important metric and using known universes to attract it, Evan Debenham's dozen yearly blog posts that gather feedback before content ships, and Ge's regret at avoiding social media and not asking for help. Then lowering friction and closing the loop: King's in-game feedback buttons and report keys, verbose patch notes crediting players, Brian Cronin's testers who become the Discord and the follow-up notes that keep them testing, Roundguard at public show-and-tells, Angband's forums improving ideas. Guidance: ship small and often, make feedback one click away, and visibly credit what you act on.

sections.heading: Reading feedback: desires, complaints and the silent majority
sections.brief: How to interpret what players tell you. Lead with the convergence that feedback is valid information but not instructions: Debenham (perspective against your own echo chamber; find the desire behind a suggestion, like Sans as a boss), Subset's three-way diagnosis of design, presentation or wanting a different game, Against the Storm's view that unpacking emotional or wrong feedback is the designer's job and that buff requests often mean a favourite playstyle, and Cole Wehrle reading every comment through reader-response theory. Then the vocal-versus-quiet problem, where Angband's maintainers, Dan DiIorio and Against the Storm converge: account for the silent content majority, wait about two weeks before reacting, and tell reflexive change resistance from genuine dislike by asking for actionable reasons (Debenham). Add sources beyond comments: watching Twitch streams for confusion (Caelyn Sandel), The Wandering Village's 6,000-person beta survey, Tyler Coleman's point that silence about the foundation is good. End with special cases: communities learning to resent overt randomness over time (Shawn Main) and Chogue facing chess players' expectations. Guidance: collect widely, diagnose before acting, and weigh the people who aren't talking.

sections.heading: Tending the space: care, moderation, volunteers and limits
sections.brief: Argue that a healthy community is cultivated, not left to form, and that the work has real costs. Lead with Ivy Melinda's framing of community management as care and cultivation with no single recipe, and Caelyn Sandel's warning that an unattended community is run by its loudest, meanest voices (and her question of who is guiding your online presence if you aren't). Then the structures Qud built: volunteer 'mayors', a wiki crew, Patreon and subreddit, with Melinda's defence of opt-in volunteering, DCSS's player-curated learndb, and Chris King's advice to answer in public so veterans repeat the answers. Then the costs and limits: King's 8 hours a week and burnout without a plan, Blaseball's user-submitted names costing moderation labour and shifting tone, Biskup's growing expectations and missed self-set deadlines, the difficulty of rekindling trust after years away, and community managers avoiding mods to stay close to the new-player experience. Guidance: budget community time, set the tone early, and give invested players defined ways to help.

sections.heading: Who the game is for: niche depth, wider audiences and newcomers
sections.brief: The central business decision: stay a niche for people who want to think hard, or reach wider. Set positions against each other: the Rogue panel and David Brevik say inherent quality need not appeal to everyone and niches can now succeed, and Scott Burger's Steam data shows traditional roguelikes hold players about 40% longer; against them Biskup argues traditional roguelikes are not mainstream-successful, that a commercial game needs more players (Ultimate ADOM), and that a wider audience means rethinking 30-year-old conventions, while Josh Ge argues polish is the main route out and Cogmind can be a bridge from roguelites. Then specific audiences: Andrea Roberts on time-poor parents, Michael Langford on children (replayable content at one skill level, the 'shame test' content toggles), Philomena Schwab on cute art signalling an easy game and drawing a mixed audience, Pokemon Mystery Dungeon reaching non-roguelike players through brand. Bring in Sandel's claim that core and new players' needs are not at odds and Streib's call to broaden access, and close on the open question of finding an audience for an unusual game (the whale-photography lightning talk). Guidance: choose the main audience deliberately, then design the presentation, accessibility and onboarding that audience needs.

sections.heading: Standing out in a crowded market: genre signals, tags and niches
sections.brief: How a roguelike gets read and found among thousands. Open with the scale: Burger's count of about 7,870 rogue-style games on Steam and Dunham's 2,554 deckbuilders. Then genre signals cut both ways: Dunham's weight-3 warning that cards on screen read as a deckbuilder and disappoint or fatigue, set against his own point that cards signal a subgenre and are easy to make look good; Zeno Rogue's observation that the roguelike label makes low-budget experiments easier to market. Then finding an underserved market: Tabea Iseli's frankly commercial choice of a non-violent cozy roguelite after Steam research, and Stray Fawn reviving Dungeon Clawler for claw-machine-loving Asian Steam audiences. Then discoverability tools: Burger's 'rogueness' tag score, tag similarity, his call for slider search and for players to vote tags, the lack of data from itch and mobile stores, Santiago Zapata's curated catalogs, Lisa Brown's motivation questions, and the 2016 warning about iOS games misusing the label. Guidance: decide what your screenshots and tags promise, and pick a niche you can describe in tags.

sections.heading: Getting found: streamers, festivals and word of mouth
sections.brief: Argue that for roguelikes, streamers and events beat social media. Lead with the convergence of Dylan Gedig (Peglin's update-stream-feedback-sales flywheel, 75,000 wishlists turning into twice that many sales) and Philomena Schwab (roguelike influencers seeking weird games drove Dungeon Clawler, not social media). Explain why roguelikes suit streaming (replayable, frequent updates, variety-streamer rotations, NetHack needing only a terminal) and the concrete playbook: enter every festival and Next Fest with a demo, demo launch tracking wishlists, a Steam key and GIF in the first email without strict embargoes, Japan-focused PR through regional partners. Add other channels: Shattered Pixel Dungeon riding an existing community into store rankings, Joe Sondow reaching people who won't download executables via Twitter bots, Caves of Qud's VTuber streams as marketing (and harassment shield), targeted key giveaways whose impact Melinda says is invisible in statistics. Close on streams as a design surface: Tyriq Plummer's failed Twitch-chat monsters and Isaac Schankler's tiny command set for crowd control. Guidance: plan updates and demos around the creators who will show them.

sections.heading: Paying for it: business models from postcardware to premium
sections.brief: How roguelike developers have actually earned (or not earned) money, and which models fit the genre. Lead with Evan Debenham's argument that ads and pay-for-advantage microtransactions cheapen a challenging roguelike and that an open-source game's community could fork it, then his ladder of revenue (cosmetic supporter extras, Patreon, finally premium on iOS once the game was worth buying). Set beside it the premium-first advice Stray Fawn got from Peglin and Luck be a Landlord developers, and Schwab's warning that simple novel designs get cloned as free-to-play mobile games. Then the history of modest returns: Rogue spreading via Unix without earning its authors money, ADOM's postcardware, Alphaman's 30 shareware registrations, Cogmind's $62,000 first year ('unpaid to poorly paid'), ADOM on Steam paying its team; plus edge cases: Jim Shepard's Steam keys for food-bank receipts and Aaron Reed's print-on-demand trouble with unique generated books. Guidance: keep monetisation away from the challenge and expect to earn the right to charge.

sections.heading: Crowdfunding: lessons from ADOM's campaign
sections.brief: Nearly all of this comes from Thomas Biskup's 2017 post-mortem of ADOM's 2012 Indiegogo campaign plus his 2016 history talk; present it as one detailed case with transferable rules, not as consensus. Lead with the weight-3 lessons: build the community first, your own outreach is the biggest donation source, set a minimal goal with stretch goals (the $48,000 goal and the post-funding surge), and promise virtual not physical rewards. Then the shape of a campaign: the valley of desperation after a fast start, weak power-pledge drives and limited rewards, the final-day surge, doubts about 60-day length, and the backlash over the amount. Then presentation and platform: 90-second video, visuals even for ASCII, professionally rewritten text, Kickstarter over Indiegogo for visibility, platform featuring worth 1.5-2%, the lost $50,000 Notch pledge, simple pledge levels. Then running and finishing: 3-5 hours of communication a day, seven contacts per backer, planning everything before launch, separating haters from critics, budgeting fees, taxes and lawyers, and fulfilment pain with physical rewards and international addresses; note the donor geography of an English-only game. Guidance: end on a short pre-launch checklist drawn from these points.

sections.heading: Who owns community work: authorship, openness and culture
sections.brief: The frontier: collective creation sits uneasily with law, commerce and authority. Lead with Kaysa Konopljak's DotA case: courts prefer singular authorship, uncredited early contributors who never policed ownership, copyright incentivising secrecy, and her claim that the roguelike community's open source and openly declared inspirations are the best defence; set beside it the NetHack DevTeam crediting MoMA only to 'the NetHack DevTeam'. Then the opposite pull: Biskup declining to open-source ADOM because it is his story and he feared fielding variant requests, shaped by death threats demanding the source. Then culture beyond the game: Tanya X. Short's society as a live-ops simulation, centralized versus grassroots change, Pixelles' ripple effect and patience over years; JP LeBreton on toolmaking as a political act; Andrew Doull's credential-free Roguelike Radio; Michael Brough on seeing games as part of all culture; Max Hawkins urging procgen skills applied to life. Guidance: decide openly what you share and how you credit contributors, and see the community as culture you help shape.
